1. **Electronics Assembly Line A** → **Functional Test (A5)**

   - 3.4s over takt (22.7% constraint)

**Rationale:**
- **Largest bottleneck margin:** 26.5% over takt is the severest constraint across all three lines

- **Highest impact per station:** A 5.3s reduction at A5 would recover substantial capacity on the highest-volume line

**Secondary priorities:**
- **Line C Injection Molding (C2):** Address the 0.45% defect rate (short_shot + flash = 60% of issues) in parallel; this can accelerate cycle time recovery
- **Line B Robotic Welding (B3):** Tackle weld_porosity (42% of defects) to reduce rework, though its constraint margin is smaller

The plant team should focus first on the Functional Test station's cycle time, then systematically address quality bottlenecks on Lines C and B to maximize overall throughput.

## Summary: Throughput Improvements with Quality Tradeoffs Visible

Here are your practical options across all three lines, with the real tradeoffs:

### **Electronics Assembly Line A** (38 uph gap)

| Option | Approach | Throughput Gain | Quality Risk | Notes |
|--------|----------|---|---|---|
| **1: Speed up Functional Test** | Process re-engineering + tooling | +23 uph | Moderate | Faster test cycles risk missing marginal failures; rework loop grows if detection window narrows |
| **2: Parallel Functional Test unit** | Duplicate bottleneck station | +32 uph | Minimal | Higher capex ($45k–$120k); OEE gains to 79.4%; quality handling stays consistent across two units |
| **3: Quality improvement** | Reduce Final Assembly defects (0.18%) | +8 uph | Negative (favorable) | Low gain but *improves* quality; reduces rework loop time—synergizes with Options 1 & 2 |

**Combined best case:** 79.4% OEE if all three run together; quality risk moderate only if test acceleration skips validation.

---

### **Metal Fabrication Line B** (39 uph gap)

| Option | Approach | Throughput Gain | Quality Risk | Notes |
|--------|----------|---|---|---|
| **1: Speed up Robotic Welding** | Process re-engineering + tooling | +23 uph | Moderate-High | Weld defects (currently 0.3%) can spike with compressed dwell times; rework costs escalate fast in metal fab |
| **2: Parallel Robotic Welding unit** | Duplicate bottleneck station | +33 uph | Minimal | $45k–$120k capex; OEE jumps to 96.1%; quality held constant; best ROI path |
| **3: Quality improvement** | Reduce Robotic Welding defects (0.3%) | +8 uph | Negative (favorable) | Already highest defect station; improving here *removes* downstream rework bottleneck |

**Combined best case:** 96.1% OEE; **warning:** Option 1 alone is risky—weld quality is fragile at speed; pair it with Option 3 or choose Option 2 for stability.

---

### **Polymer Molding Line C** (72 uph gap — largest opportunity)

| Option | Approach | Throughput Gain | Quality Risk | Notes |
|--------|----------|---|---|---|
| **1: Speed up Injection Molding** | Process re-engineering + tooling | +43 uph | High | Reduced cooling/cure cycles = warping, shrinkage, dimensional drift; defect rate (0.45%) will likely jump to 0.8%+ unless validated |
| **2: Parallel Injection Molding unit** | Duplicate bottleneck station | +61 uph | Minimal | Largest throughput win; $45k–$120k capex; OEE improves to 76.2%; quality stays controlled |
| **3: Quality improvement** | Reduce Injection Molding defects (0.45%) | +14 uph | Negative (favorable) | Highest defect station; improving here also removes rework queuing; best complementary move |

**Combined best case:** 76.2% OEE if all three run; **Polymer C is the most aggressive—** Option 1 alone will hurt quality unless material science and mold design are re-validated.

---

## My Audit Take

**Which option to push first:**
1. **Short-term (quality-safe):** Option 3 (Quality improvement) on all lines—reduces rework, gains 8–14 uph each with *no throughput–quality tradeoff*.
2. **Medium-term (balanced):** Option 2 (Parallel station) on your worst bottleneck—Polymer C needs it most (61 uph gain); Electronics A and Metal B come second.
3. **Long-term (risky if rushed):** Option 1 (Speed process)—only after quality improvement anchors the defect floor, and only with material/mold/parameter re-validation.

**Bottom line:** Metal Fab Line B is the cleanest win (96.1% OEE with parallel unit). Polymer Line C needs both capital *and* process engineering care. Don't accelerate Injection Molding without validating dimensional stability first—that defect rate will spike.

What's your priority: capex availability, quality floor, or nearest-term volume?
